column3: It explicitly joins the failure of excuses to the refusal of later reconciliation, directly clarifying the focus verse's final closure.
Entry through Hell's gates and abiding there makes the focus's mathwa a settled, enduring destination.
Patient righteous action and its reward contrast with the focus's futile endurance after punishment has already become fixed.
It adds that neither departure from the Fire nor renewed favor is available, matching both closures in the focus.
The immediate surah context names the Fire as the eternal home of those who reject the signs.
Its enduring Hell-residence repeats the destination in the focus, but adds little after 40:76.
It independently states that disbelievers are neither permitted to speak nor allowed to seek restored favor.
The arrogance and rejection of signs in the same surah identify conduct leading into the punishment described at the focus.
It confirms Hell as the lodging of disbelievers, reinforcing the focus's use of mathwa.
The contrast between believers' gardens and the Fire as the disbelievers' lodging frames the focus's destination morally.
Preparation of Hell for hostile doubters supplies a general punitive setting without explaining endurance or reconciliation.
It portrays patience as a deliberate, living allegiance, contrasting with the focus's involuntary endurance in the Fire.
Turning away from belief gives a broad antecedent to the focus's judgment, without its finality.
The same surah's steadfast believers receive freedom from fear and the Garden, a pointed contrast to 41:24.
Its commendation of the patient supplies only a general positive contrast to futile post-judgment patience.
It repeats Hell as a lodging for deniers but is already covered by stronger residence verses.
The warning of a destructive punishment in the same surah supplies a proximate antecedent to the focus's outcome.
Patient gratitude amid altered circumstances is only a distant contrast to endurance after irreversible punishment.
Satisfaction and resentment over charity faintly echo seeking favor, but remain a worldly dispute.
Being tested upon the Fire supplies a concise punishment scene that precedes the focus's settled residence.
Patience before demanding another's emergence shows a timely, voluntary restraint, contrasting with the focus's too-late appeal.
It distinguishes repentance while open from turning away into painful punishment, clarifying the temporal stakes of the focus.
Angelic patronage and fulfilled desire in the next surah passage contrast with the condemned having no restored favor.
Beautiful patience gives the living, commanded form of patience that the focus contrasts with endurance after judgment.
It names the Fire as the lodging of wrongdoers, but repeats an already established destination.
The Quran's detailed Arabic exposition does not add to the Fire, patience, or refusal of restored favor.
Patience and God-consciousness protecting against hostile plans only broadly contrast with the focus's final condition.
The absence of rescue in a drowning scene gives only a remote image of helplessness.
Preference for the final abode and its reward is a broad positive alternative to the focus's punishment.
Battlefield patience conditioned for aid does not materially clarify final punishment.
Its question about enduring the Fire sharply reverses the focus's statement that their endurance cannot alter their abode.
The merciful welcome offered to believers in the same passage is only a brief contrast to the Fire's lodging.
Patience joined to reliance before judgment contrasts with the focus's endurance when no reversal remains.
The Fire as the deniers' promised meeting supplies only general destination context.
The same surah calls for steadfast turning and forgiveness before warning the associators, directly contrasting the closed appeal in 41:24.
Willing patience in a trial is a remote contrast to compelled endurance in punishment.
Human ingratitude after mercy and adversity supplies a general cause for punishment, not the focus's finality.
The command to taste the punishment depicts its realized, deserved character, supporting the Fire scene in the focus.
Patience for the Lord supplies a purposeful pre-judgment counterpart to patience that no longer changes anything.
The question about their failure to believe is only a broad antecedent to judgment.
The same surah's unfailing reward for believers provides a nearby opposite outcome to the Fire's fixed lodging.
A promise to be patient under instruction is not closely related to final punishment.
Rescue from a worldly fire contrasts only distantly with the inescapable Fire in the focus.
Creation and return to God give broad eschatological context without explaining the focus's closure.
Seeking help through patience and prayer is a general pre-judgment alternative to futile endurance.
Steadfastness under hardship supplies only a general contrast to punishment endurance.
The same surah links disbelief to deafness, blindness, and a distant call, supplying a nearby antecedent to its punishment.
Inability to remain patient in a teaching encounter does not illuminate the Fire or rejected reconciliation.
The lack of intercessors explains one dimension of the condemned group's inability to obtain relief or restored favor.
A believer's declaration of faith does not add a focused relation after the prior contrasts.
Prayer for steadfastness in battle is a general example of useful patience before an outcome.
Layered darkness and lack of divine light offer only an indirect image of the deniers' state.
Joseph's earthly establishment does not clarify the focus's final punishment.
Patience until God judges separates meaningful waiting before judgment from the focus's endurance after it.
The legal rulings on emigrant women do not contribute to the focus's eschatological closure.
The superiority of the afterlife reward is too general to add to the established contrast.
Patience through measured trial is a broad pre-judgment contrast to the focus's irreversible punishment.
It explicitly says they seek to leave the Fire but cannot, directly sharpening the permanence of the focus's mathwa.
It makes the Fire an enduring lodging after mutual worldly enjoyment, closely matching the focus's settled abode.
The Garden given for patience shows the positive outcome of patience exercised before judgment, opposed to 41:24.
The lowest depth of the Fire and absence of any helper reinforce the condemned condition's lack of remedy.
The reciprocal alliance of wrongdoers gives background for culpable association but not the focus's closure.
Patience as one element of righteous conduct is already represented by more specific positive contrasts.
Remembering God after temptation is a distant alternative to persisting toward punishment.
The threatened ascent conveys severity but not residence, endurance, or rejected favor.
Forgiveness after migration, striving, and patience marks repentance and endurance while remedy remains possible.
It acknowledges God's authority to punish or forgive, but does not specify the focus's final refusal.
Stubborn resistance to the signs gives a proximate cause for the punitive closure described in the focus.
Peaceful arrival at the good abode because of patience provides a precise positive counterpart to the Fire as lodging.
Inability to go forward or return forms a useful image of being immobilized without a way back.
Punishment of criminals and aid for believers give only general retributive context.
Mutual counsel in patience places patience within an active saving practice, contrasting with its impotence after judgment.
Persistent unbelief despite warning is a broad antecedent, not an account of punishment's finality.
Divine companionship with the patient is a general positive contrast already supplied more specifically above.
The disbelievers' inability to ward Fire from themselves and lack of aid reinforce their helplessness in punishment.
Patient forgiveness describes a voluntary moral response before judgment, contrasting with a later unavailable request for favor.
It supplies the embodied suffering of those in the Fire, extending the focus's statement of their abode.
The river test and patient minority offer only a remote example of pre-judgment steadfastness.
The punished arrogant find neither protector nor helper, reinforcing the focus's absence of a remedial relationship.
God's knowledge of each person's movements and final lodging supports the focus's destination as a known terminus.
The Fire encloses wrongdoers and their appeal for relief receives a scalding response, vividly developing the focus's irreversible condition.
This repeated teaching-scene statement adds no further relation beyond 18:67.
Hell as the lodging of the arrogant repeats the focus's destination with the added exposure of humiliation at resurrection.
Patient worship is a general pre-judgment contrast without further connection to the Fire scene.
Being cast into Hell supplies a general entry image, already covered by more explicit residence verses.
Patience until God's judgment makes clear that patience has force before the judgment the focus portrays as completed.
The command to enter Hell's gates and abide there repeats the focus's permanent lodging, with limited marginal addition.
It directly declares that endurance or non-endurance in the Fire is alike, the closest explanation of 41:24's first clause.
No protectors and no path after divine misguidance reinforce the focus's lack of a route back to favor.
Patience and gratitude in reading a sign of navigation do not clarify the final Fire scene.
The inevitability of death supplies only distant eschatological context.
Messengerly patience until divine help arrives contrasts with the focus's endurance after the time for help has passed.
Pre-dawn seeking forgiveness is too brief and general after the stronger timely-repentance contrasts.
Patient certainty producing leadership is a remote positive use of patience.
Gardens for the God-conscious provide only a general opposite outcome.
Patience and gratitude in contemplating ships do not add to the focus's punishment.
The account of sorcery and harmful learning has no focused relation to endurance in the Fire or rejected reconciliation.
At judgment the leaders admit that panic and patience are alike because no escape remains, directly paralleling the focus.
Naming exemplary patient figures adds no marginal understanding of the focus.
Patient God-consciousness receiving reward offers a final broad contrast to endurance after punishment is fixed.
The immediately preceding verse identifies their destructive expectation about their Lord as the cause of becoming losers, directly setting up the fixed outcome in 41:24.
The following verse explains that evil companions made their deeds seem fair and that the decree of punishment became due, supplying the causal continuation of the focus.
Disowned followers see the punishment and say that, if returned, they would disown their leaders; it joins regret, severed support, and an inescapable punishment.
Abiding under the curse with neither punishment lightened nor reprieve granted closely develops the focus's irreversible condition.
At the Fire, the deniers wish they could be returned and become believers, supplying a concrete belated reversal wish before its refusal is established elsewhere.
It explicitly describes the wretched as abiding in the Fire, articulating the duration implicit in the focus's mathwa.
The condemned face a drink they can barely swallow while death does not come to them, clarifying why mere endurance offers no release.
The criminal in Hell neither dies nor lives, giving a direct account of punishment as a state from which endurance cannot resolve itself.
Whenever they seek to leave the Fire because of anguish, they are returned to it, directly answering the focus's closed possibility of change.
The people of the Fire ask to be brought out and promise righteous conduct, the closest explicit parallel to a belated appeal for reversal.
The answer commands them to remain in the Fire and denies them further address, directly states the outcome left implicit in the focus.
Criminals confess, acknowledge sight and hearing, and ask to be sent back for good deeds, a close parallel to too-late remorse and requested reversal.
The people of the Fire neither die nor have punishment reduced, directly explains the futility of their endurance.
The disbelievers acknowledge two deaths and two lives and ask whether any way out remains, forming the closest same-surah counterpart to a final request for escape.
It gives the reason the requested exit is denied: they disbelieved when God alone was invoked.
Those in the Fire ask its keepers to seek even one day of reduced punishment, showing the constrained plea that follows fixed condemnation.
The keepers answer that the disbelievers' supplication goes astray after the proofs came, directly limiting appeals made from within the Fire.
The criminals remain in the punishment of Hell, an explicit enduring-state counterpart to the focus's mathwa.
Their punishment is not lightened and they despair within it, directly extending the focus's finality.
Their appeal to the keeper of Hell for death is answered with remaining there, a direct instance of an appeal that cannot end the punishment.
No ransom is accepted and the Fire is declared their refuge, reinforcing the focus's closure of remedial alternatives.
